mad.e: From Middle English mad, madde, madd, medd, from Old English ġemǣd, ġemǣded (“enraged”), past participle of ġemǣdan, *mǣdan (“to make insane or foolish”), from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną (“to change; damage; cripple; injure; make mad”), from Proto-Germanic *maidaz ("weak; crippled".

made.e: From Middle English made, makede, makode (preterite) and maad, mad, maked (past participle), from Old English macode (first and third person preterite) and macod, gemacode, ġemacod (past participle), from macian (“to make”).

madman.e: From Middle English mad-man. By surface analysis, mad + -man.
madman.g: A man who is insane or mentally disturbed.

madness.e: From Middle English madnes, madnesse; equivalent to mad + -ness.
madness.g: The state of being mad; insanity; mental disease.

mag.e: From Mag, a nickname for Margaret.

maggot.e: From Middle English magot, magat, maked, probably a metathetic alteration of maddock, maðek (“worm", "maggot”), originally a diminutive form of a base represented by Old English maþa (Scots mathe), from Proto-West Germanic *maþō, from Proto-Germanic *maþô, from the Proto-Indo-European root *mat, which was used in insect names, equivalent to made + -ock.
maggot.g: A soft, legless larva of a fly or other dipteran insect, that often eats decomposing organic matter.

magic.e: From Middle English magik, magyk, from Old French magique (noun and adjective), from Latin magicus (adjective), magica (noun use of feminine form of magicus), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós, “magical”), from μάγος (mágos, “magician, magus”). Ultimately from Old Iranian, probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂gʰ- (“to be able to, to help.
magic.g: The application of rituals or actions, especially those based on occult knowledge, to subdue or manipulate natural or supernatural beings an

magician.e: From Middle English magicien, from Middle French magicien.
magician.g: A person who plays with or practices allegedly supernatural magic.

magistrate.e: From Middle English magistrat, maiestrat (“magistrate; magistracy”), borrowed from Latin magistrātus.
magistrate.g: A judicial officer with limited authority to administer and enforce the law. A magistrate's court may have jurisdiction in civil or criminal

magnificence.e: From Middle English magnificence, from Old French magnificence, from Latin magnificentia.

magnificent.e: From Middle English magnificent, from Middle French magnificent, from Latin magnificentior, comparative of magnificus (“great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid, etc.”), from magnus (“great”) + -ficēns, a form of -ficiēns, the regular form, in compounds, of faciēns, a participle of facere (“to do”).
magnificent.g: Grand, elegant or splendid in appearance.

magnify.e: From Middle English magnifien, from Middle French magnifier, from Latin magnificāre, from magnificus.
magnify.g: To praise, glorify (someone or something, especially God).

magnitude.g: The absolute or relative size, extent or importance of something.

maid.e: From Middle English mayde, maide, abbreviation of Middle English maiden from Old English mæġden (Old English mǣden). Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *magaþ, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs (“girl, virgin”).
maid.g: A girl or an unmarried young woman; maiden.

maiden.e: From Middle English mayden, meiden, from Old English mæġden (“girl”), originally a diminutive of mæġeþ (“girl”) via diminutive suffix -en, from Proto-West Germanic *magaþ, from Proto-Germanic *magaþs. Equivalent to maid + -en.
maiden.g: A girl or an unmarried young woman.

maidservant.e: From Middle English maide servant; equivalent to maid + servant.

mail.e: From Middle English male, from Anglo-Norman male, Old French male (“bag, wallet”), from Frankish *malha (“bag”), from Proto-Germanic *malhō (“bag, pouch”), from Proto-Indo-European *molko- (“leather pouch”).

From Middle English mayle (“mail armor”), borrowed from Old French maille (“loop, stitch”), from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish, mesh”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *smh₁-tleh₂, from *smeh₁- (“smear, rub”).
mail.g: Armour consisting of metal rings linked together.

maim.e: From Middle English maymen, mahaymen, from Anglo-Norman maheimer, mahaigner, of Germanic origin; see mayhem.
maim.g: To wound seriously; to cause permanent loss of function of a limb or part of the body.

maimed.e: From Middle English maymed, ymaymed. By surface analysis, maim + -ed.
maimed.g: Partially or wholly deprived of the use of some part of the body, usually by wounding or injury.

main.e: From Middle English mayn, main, maine, mæin, meyn, from main (noun) (see further at etymology 2); compare Old English mæġen (“strong, main, principal”) (used in combination) and Old Norse megn, megenn (“strong, main”).
main.g: Of chief or leading importance; prime, principal.

main.e: From Middle English mayn, main, maine, mæine, mæȝen, from Old English mæġen (“strength”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą (“strength, power, might”), *maginaz (“strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“be able”). The word is cognate with Old High German magen, megin, Old Norse magn, megn, megin, Old Saxon megin.
main.g: That which is chief or principal; the chief or main portion; the bulk, the greater part, gross.

mainland.e: From Middle English mayne londe; equivalent to main + land.
mainland.g: The continent; the principal land, as distinguished from islands or a peninsula.

mainsail.g: The largest (or only) sail on a sailing vessel.

mainstay.e: From Middle English main stai, equivalent to main + stay (“rope”).

maintain.e: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manūteneō, manūtenēre (“I support”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”, ablative of manus) + tenēre (“to hold”).
maintain.g: To keep up; to preserve; to uphold (a state, condition etc.).

maintenance.e: From Middle English mayntenaunce, from Old French maintenance, from maintenir, from Latin manus tenēre (“to hold in the hand”). By surface analysis, maintain + -ance. Note that maintain has undergone a sound and spelling change, hence is spelt with -tain-, rather than the -ten- still found in maintenance.
maintenance.g: Actions performed to keep some machine or system functioning or in service.

majestic.g: Having qualities of splendor or royalty.

majesty.e: From Middle English majeste, mageste, from Old French majesté, from Latin maiestātem, (literally, "the quality of being greater”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂s (“great”) See mega-.
majesty.g: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.

major.e: From Middle English major, from Latin maior, comparative of magnus (“great, large; noble, important”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs (“greater”), comparative of *meǵh₂- (“great”). Noun sense 1 is a shortening of sergeant major, perhaps after Spanish mayor in the same sense.
major.g: Greater in dignity, rank, importance, significance, or interest.

majority.e: From Middle French maiorité, from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + -ity.
majority.g: More than half (50%) of some group.

make.e: From Middle English maken, make, from Old English macian (“to build, make, work”), from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to build, make, work”), from *mak (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ-, *meh₂ḱ- (“to knead”) or *meg- (“to be comfortable, pleasant”).

make.g: An agricultural tool resembling a scythe, used to cut (harvest) certain plants such as peas, reeds, or tares.

maker.e: From Middle English maker, makere, equivalent to make + -er.
maker.g: Someone who makes; a person or thing that makes or produces something.

making.e: From Middle English making, from Old English macung (“making”), equivalent to make + -ing.
making.g: The act of forming, causing, or constituting; workmanship; construction.

male.e: From Middle English male, borrowed from Old French malle, masle (Modern French mâle), from Latin masculus (“masculine, a male”), diminutive of mās (“male, masculine”).
male.g: One of the male (masculine) sex or gender.

malefactor.e: From Middle English malefactour, from Late Latin malefactor, from Latin malefaciō, from male (“evilly”) + factus (“made or done”), past participle of facio (“to make or do”).

malice.e: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).
malice.g: Intention to harm or deprive in an illegal or immoral way. Desire to take pleasure in another's misfortune.

malicious.e: From Middle English malicious, from Old French malicios, from Latin malitiōsus, from malitia (“malice”), from malus (“bad”). By surface analysis, malice + -ious.
malicious.g: Intending to do harm; characterized by spite and malice.

maliciously.e: From Middle English maliciousli; equivalent to malicious + -ly.
maliciously.g: In a malicious manner, or for malicious reasons.

maliciousness.e: From Middle English maliciousnes; equivalent to malicious + -ness.
maliciousness.g: The condition of being malicious; malevolence or malice.

malign.e: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”).
malign.g: Evil or malignant in disposition, nature, intent or influence.

malignant.e: From Middle French malignant, from Late Latin malignans.

malignity.e: From Middle English malignete, malignitee, malignyte, malyngnite, from Middle French maligneté, from Latin malignitās. By surface analysis, malign + -ity. (a group of goblins): Coined by David Malki in the 30 October 2009 Wondermark webcomic strip “Supernatural Collective Nouns”.
malignity.g: The quality of being malign or malignant; badness, evilness, monstrosity, depravity, maliciousness.

mallow.e: From Middle English malwe, from Old English mealwe, borrowed from Latin malva.
mallow.g: Any of a group of flowering plants in several genera of the taxonomic family Malvaceae, especially of the genus Malva. Several species are e

man.e: From Middle English man, from Old English mann m (“human being, person, man”), from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *mon- (“human being, man”). Virtually all the words below mean “man” and “husband”, with some specific cases noted.
From Middle English mannen, from Old English mannian, ġemannian (“to man, supply with men, populate, garrison”), from mann (“human being, man”).
man.g: To supply (something) with staff or crew (of either sex).

man-made.e: From man (“human”) + made. According to the OED, the pronunciation with primary stress on man, /ˈmænˌmeɪd/, is older.
man-made.g: Created or caused by human beings, as opposed to occurring in nature; artificial or synthetic.

manage.e: From Early Modern English manage, menage, from Middle English *manage, *menage, from Old French manege (“the handling or training of a horse, horsemanship, riding, maneuvers, proceedings”), probably from Old Italian maneggiare (“to handle, manage, touch, treat”), from Vulgar Latin *manizāre (“handle”).
manage.g: To direct or be in charge of.

mandrake.e: From Middle English mandrake, mandroke, an alteration of mandragora with the ending -dragora reinterpreted as related to dragon and replaced with native drake, from Old English mandragora, from Medieval Latin mandragorās, from Ancient Greek μανδραγόρας (mandragóras).
mandrake.g: Any plant of the genus Mandragora, certain of which are said to have medicinal or aphrodisiac properties; the root of these plants often res

mane.e: From Middle English mane, mayne, from Old English manu (“mane”), from Proto-West Germanic *manu, from Proto-Germanic *manō (“mane”), from Proto-Indo-European *mony-, *mon- (“neck”).
mane.g: Longer hair growth on back of neck of an animal, especially a horse or lion.

mane.e: Dialectal rendering of man, as used in African-American Vernacular English.

manger.e: From Middle English manger, from Old French mangeoire, menjoere, from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger).
manger.g: A trough in a stable or barn for animals to eat from.

manifest.e: From Middle English manifest, manifeste, from Latin manifestus, manufestus (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + an uncertain second element.
manifest.g: Evident to the senses, especially to the sight; apparent; distinctly perceived.

manifestation.e: From Middle English manifestacion, manyfestacion, manyfestacioun; from Late Latin manifestātiō. In the political sense, a semantic loan from French manifestation. By surface analysis, manifest + -ation.
manifestation.g: The act or process of becoming manifest.

manifold.e: From Middle English manifold, from Old English maniġfeald (“manifold, various, varied, complicated, numerous, abundant, plural”), from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz, equivalent to many + -fold.
manifold.g: Various in kind, quality, or manifestation; diverse.

manifold.e: From Middle English manifolden, from Old English maniġfealdan (“to multiply, abound, increase, extend, reward”), equivalent to many + -fold.

mankind.e: From Middle English mankynde, alteration (due to kynde = “kind, nature, sort”) of earlier mankyn, from Old English mancynn. Equivalent to man + kin, and/or man + -kind.
mankind.g: The human race in its entirety.

manna.e: From Middle English, from Old English, from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מן (mān, “'manna”).
manna.g: Food miraculously produced for the Israelites in the desert in the book of Exodus.
manna.sf: From Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מן (mān, “manna”)

manner.e: From Middle English manere, maner, from Anglo-Norman manere, from Old French maniere, from Vulgar Latin *manāria, from feminine of Latin manuarius (“belonging to the hand”), from manus (“hand”).
manner.g: Mode of action; way of performing or doing anything.

manservant.e: From Middle English man servant, man servaunt; equivalent to man + servant.

mansion.e: From Middle English mansioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mansion, mansiun, from Latin mānsiō (“dwelling, stopping-place”), from the past participle stem of manēre (“stay”). By surface analysis, manse + -ion.
mansion.g: A large luxurious house or building, usually built for the wealthy.

manslayer.e: From Middle English mansleere, man-slere, manslaer, from Old English mannslaga, equivalent to man + slayer.
manslayer.g: One who commits homicide or manslaughter

mantle.e: From Middle English mantel, from Old English mæntel, mentel (“sleeveless cloak”), from Proto-West Germanic *mantel; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman mantel, both from Latin mantellum (“covering, cloak”) (French manteau), diminutive of mantum (Spanish manto), probably from Gaulish *mantos, *mantalos (“trodden road”), from Proto-Celtic *mantos, *mantlos.
mantle.g: A piece of clothing somewhat like an open robe or cloak, especially that worn by Orthodox bishops.

manure.e: From Middle English maynouren, manuren (“to supervise, toil”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman meinourer and Old French manovrer (whence also English maneuver, or in French manœuvrer) from Vulgar Latin *manuoperare (“work by hand”), from Latin manū (“by hand”) + operārī (“to work”).
manure.g: To cultivate by manual labor; to till; hence, to develop by culture.

many.e: From Middle English many, mani, moni, from Old English maniġ, moniġ, maneġ (“many”), from Proto-West Germanic *manag, from Proto-Germanic *managaz (“many; much”), from Proto-Indo-European *menegʰ-, *mengʰ- (“many, sufficient”) or Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂- (“big, great”).
many.g: before a countable noun: A large, indefinite number of.

map.e: Shortening or back-formation of Middle English mappemounde, mapemounde (“world map”), from Old French mapamonde, from Medieval Latin mappa mundī, compound of Latin mappa (“napkin, cloth”) and mundus (“world”).
map.g: A visual representation of an area, whether real or imaginary, showing the relative positions of places and other features.

mar.e: From Middle English merren, from Old English mierran (“to mar, disturb, confuse; scatter, squander, waste; upset, hinder, obstruct; err”), from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną (“to disturb, hinder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mers- (“to annoy, disturb, neglect, forget, ignore”).
mar.g: To spoil; to ruin; to scathe; to damage.
Alternative form of mere (“a body of standing water”).

marble.e: From Middle English marble, marbre; from Anglo-Norman and Old French marbre, from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros), perhaps related to μαρμάρεος (marmáreos, “gleaming”). The forms from French displaced Old English marma, which had previously been borrowed from Latin.
marble.g: A metamorphic rock of crystalline limestone.

march.e: From Middle English marchen, from Middle French marcher (“to march, walk”), from Old French marchier (“to stride, to march, to trample”), from Frankish *markōn (“to mark, mark out, to press with the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *markōną (“to mark”).
march.g: A formal, rhythmic way of walking, used especially by soldiers, by bands, and in ceremonies.

march.e: From Middle English marche (“tract of land along a country's border”), from Old French marche (“boundary, frontier”), from Frankish *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō, from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary”).
march.g: A border region, especially one originally set up to defend a boundary.

mare.e: From Middle English mare, meare, meir, mer, mere, meyre, mure, from Old English mīere (“female horse, mare”), from Proto-West Germanic *marhijā, from Proto-Germanic *marhijō (“female horse”), from *marhaz (“horse”), from Proto-Indo-European *márkos (“horse”).

From Middle English mare, from Old English mare (“nightmare, monster”), from Proto-West Germanic *marā, from Proto-Germanic *marǭ (“nightmare, incubus”), from Proto-Indo-European *mor- (“feminine evil spirit”). After becoming obsolete in its original usage, the term was recreated in modern colloquial speech as a clipping of the derived term nightmare.
mare.g: A type of evil spirit formerly thought to sit on the chest of a sleeping person; also, the feeling of suffocation felt during sleep, attribu

mariner.e: From Middle English mariner, maryner, from Anglo-Norman mariner, marinier, from Old French marinier, maronnier, from marin and Medieval Latin marinellus and marinarius (“sailor”), from marīnus (“marine”), from mare (“sea”) + -īnus (“-ine: forming adjectives”).
mariner.g: Synonym of sailor, particularly one on a maritime vessel.

marish.e: From Middle English mareys, marys, from Anglo-Norman mareis, mereis, or from Middle French mares, marest, both from Late Latin mariscus, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk (“marsh”).

marital.e: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

maritime.e: Borrowed from Middle French maritime, from Latin maritimus.
maritime.g: Relating to or connected with the sea or its uses (as navigation, commerce, etc.).

mark.e: From Middle English mark, merk, merke, from Old English mearc (“mark, sign, line of division; standard; boundary, limit, term, border; defined area, district, province”), from Proto-West Germanic *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary; boundary marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary, border”).
From Middle English mark, from Old English marc (“a denomination of weight (usu. half a pound), mark (money of account)”), from Proto-West Germanic *mark, from Proto-Germanic *marką (“mark, sign”).
mark.g: A half pound, a traditional unit of mass equivalent to 226.8 g.

marked.e: From mark (“sign, characteristic, visible impression”) + -ed. Less common disyllabic pronunciation (/ˈmɑː.kɪd/) is likely an analogy derived from markedness (explaining its restriction to sense 2).
marked.g: Having a visible or identifying mark.

market.e: From Middle English market, from late Old English market (“market”) and Anglo-Norman markiet (Old French marchié); all ultimately from Latin mercātus (“trade, market”), from mercor (“to trade, deal in, buy”), itself derived from merx (“wares, merchandise”).
market.g: A gathering of people for the purchase and sale of merchandise, often periodic at a set time.

marketplace.g: An open area in a town housing a public market.

marred.e: From Middle English marred, merred (“troubled, distressed, vexed, bewildered”), from Old English *mierred, ġemyrred (“disturbed, troubled”), past participle of Old English mierran, ġemyrran (“to hinder, obstruct, force, trouble, err”), equivalent to mar + -ed.

marriage.e: From Middle English mariage, from Old French mariage, from marier (“to marry”), from Latin marītō (“marry”, verb, literally “give in marriage”), from marītus (“lover”, “nuptial”), from mas (“male, masculine, of the male sex”). Equivalent to marry + -age.

married.e: From Middle English maried, imaried, mariet, past participle of Middle English marien (“to marry”), equivalent to marry + -ed.
married.g: In a state of marriage; having a wife or a husband.

marrow.e: From Middle English mary, marow, marwe, marowȝ, from Old English mearg, from Proto-West Germanic *maʀg, from Proto-Germanic *mazgą, *mazgaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰos.
marrow.g: The substance inside bones which produces blood cells.

marry.e: From Middle English marien, from Anglo-Norman marïer, from Latin marītāre (“to wed”), from marītus (“husband, suitor”), from mās (“man, male”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *méryos (“young man”), same source as Sanskrit मर्य (márya, “suitor, young man”).
marry.g: To enter into the conjugal or connubial state; to take a husband or a wife.

marry.e: From Middle English Marie, referring to Mary, the Virgin Mary. Mid-14th century.
marry.g: A term of asseveration: indeed!, in truth!

marsh.e: From Middle English mersch, from Old English mersċ, merisċ, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk, derived from *mari, equivalent to mere (“sea, body of water”) + -ish.
marsh.g: An area of low, wet land, often with tall grass or herbaceous plants.

mart.e: From Middle Dutch mart, markt (“market”) (Modern Dutch markt), from Old Dutch *markat, from Late Latin marcātus, an alternative form of Classical Latin mercātus.
mart.g: A shop, a store, a market.

martyr.e: From Middle English martir, from Old English martyr, itself a borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
martyr.g: One who willingly accepts being put to death or willingly accepts challenging and exposing iniquity done to oneself for adhering openly to o

marvellously.e: From Middle English merveilously; equivalent to marvellous + -ly.

mason.e: From Middle English masoun, machun, from Anglo-Norman machun, masson, Old French maçon, from Late Latin maciō (“carpenter, bricklayer”).
mason.g: A bricklayer, one whose occupation is to build with stone or brick.

masonry.e: From Middle English masonry, masonrie, partly from Old French maçonerie and partly from mason + -ry.
masonry.g: The art or occupation of a mason.

masquerade.e: Maschera is derived from Medieval Latin masca (“mask”): see further there. The English word is cognate with Late Latin masquarata, Portuguese mascarada, Spanish mascarada.
masquerade.g: An assembly or party of people wearing (usually elaborate or fanciful) masks and costumes, and amusing themselves with dancing, conversation

mass.e: In late Middle English (circa 1400) as masse in the sense of "lump, quantity of matter", from Anglo-Norman masse, in Old French attested from the 11th century, via late Latin massa (“lump, dough”), from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley-cake, lump (of dough)”).

From Middle English messe, masse, from Old English mæsse (“the mass, church festival”) and Old French messe, from Vulgar Latin *messa (“Eucharist, dismissal”), from Late Latin missa, noun use of feminine past participle of classical Latin mittere (“to send”).
mass.g: The Eucharist, now especially in Roman Catholicism.

massive.e: From Middle English massif, from Middle French massif, equivalent to mass + -ive. The Irish sense is possibly derived from Irish mas (“fine, handsome”).
massive.g: Very large in size or extent.

mast.e: From Middle English mast, from Old English mæst (“mast”), from Proto-West Germanic *mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz (“mast, sail-pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *mazdos (“pole, mast”).
mast.g: A tall, slim post or tower, usually tapering upward, used to support, for example, sails or observation platforms on a ship, the main rotor

mast.e: From French masse, with -t probably after Etymology 1, above.
mast.g: A type of heavy cue, with the broad end of which one strikes the ball.

master.e: From Middle English maister, mayster, meister (noun) and maistren (verb), from Old English mǣster, mæġster, mæġester, mæġister, magister (“master”), from Latin magister (“chief, teacher, leader”), from Old Latin magester.
master.g: Someone who has control over something or someone.

mastery.e: From Middle English maistery, maistrie, mastere, mastry, from Old French maistrie, equivalent to master + -y.
mastery.g: The position or authority of a master; dominion; command; supremacy; superiority.

mat.e: From Middle English matte (“mat”), from Old English meatte (“mat”), from Late Latin matta (“mat made of rushes”), from Punic or Phoenician (compare Hebrew מיטה \ מִטָּה (mitá, “bed, couch”)).
mat.g: A flat piece of coarse material used for wiping one’s feet, or as a decorative or protective floor covering.

mat.e: Borrowed from Russian мат (mat), abbreviated from the expression ма́терная брань (máternaja branʹ), ultimately from мать (matʹ, “mother”).
mat.g: Vulgar, obscene, or profane language in Russian and some other Slavic language communities.

match.e: From Middle English macche, mecche, from Old English mæċċa, ġemæċċa (“companion, mate, wife, one suited to another”), from Proto-West Germanic *makkjō, *gamakkjō (“partner, equal”), from Proto-Germanic *makô, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, work”).
match.g: Any contest or trial of strength or skill, or to determine superiority.

match.e: From Middle English macchen (“to marry; be paired with”), from the noun (see above).
match.g: To agree; to be equal; to correspond.

mate.e: From Middle English mate, a borrowing from Middle Low German mate (“messmate”) (replacing Middle English mett, mette (“table companion, mate, partner”), from Old English ġemetta (“sharer of food, table-guest”)).
mate.g: A fellow, comrade, colleague, partner or someone with whom something is shared, e.g. shipmate, classmate.

mate.e: From Middle English maten (“to overpower”), from Old French mater (“to kill”), from Vulgar Latin *mattō, of unclear origin.

material.e: From Middle English material, from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”), from māter (“mother”).
material.g: Of, relating to, or consisting of matter, especially physical.

matrix.e: From Middle English matris, matrice, matrix, from Old French matrice (“pregnant animal”), or from Latin mātrīx (“dam, womb”), both ultimately from māter (“mother”). Slang usage coined with the 1999 sci-fi action film The Matrix.
matrix.g: The cavity or mold in which anything is formed.

matter.e: From Middle English matere, mater, from Anglo-Norman matere, materie, from Old French materie, matiere, from Latin māteria (“wood”), from māter (“mother”), in which case cognate with Old Armenian մայր (mayr, “cedar”) and մայրի (mayri, “forest”).

mattock.e: From Middle English mattok (“mattock, pickaxe”), from Old English mattuc, meottoc, mettoc (“mattock, fork, trident”), from Proto-West Germanic *mattjuk (“mattock, ploughshare”), from Proto-Indo-European *met- (“to cut, reap”).
mattock.g: An agricultural tool whose blades are at right angles to the body, similar to a pickaxe.

mature.e: From late Middle English mature, from Middle French mature, from Latin mātūrus. Partially displaced ripe, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”).
mature.g: Fully developed; grown up in terms of physical appearance, behaviour or thinking; ripe.

mature.e: From Middle English maturen, from Middle French maturer (“to mature”), from Latin mātūrō.
mature.g: To proceed toward maturity: full development or completion (either of concrete or of abstract things, e.g. plans, judgments, qualities).

maturity.e: From Middle English maturitee, maturyte, from Old French maturité, from Latin mātūritātem. By surface analysis, mature + -ity.
maturity.g: The state of being mature, ready or ripe; the prime state of productibility and self expression.

maul.e: From Middle English malle (“mace, maul”), from Anglo-Norman mail, from Old French mail, from Latin malleus (“hammer”).
maul.g: A heavy long-handled hammer, used for splitting logs by driving a wedge into them, or in combat.

maw.e: From Middle English mawe, maghe, maȝe, from Old English maga (“stomach; maw”), from Proto-West Germanic *magō, from Proto-Germanic *magô (“belly; stomach”), from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks- (“bag, bellows, belly”).
maw.g: The upper digestive tract (where food enters the body), especially the mouth and jaws of an animal.

maxim.e: From Anglo-Norman maxime and Middle French maxime, from Late Latin maxima (“axiom”), noun use of the feminine singular form of Latin maximus (apparently as used in the phrase prōpositiō maxima (“greatest premise”)).
maxim.g: A self-evident axiom or premise; a pithy expression of a general principle or rule.

maxim.e: Named after American and British inventor Hiram Maxim (1840–1916).

may.e: From Middle English magen, mauen, mawe, mawen, mayen, maȝen, mouin, mow, mowen, moȝen, mugen, from Old English magan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”).
may.g: To be strong; to have power (over).

may.e: From Middle English may, maye (“woman, maid, girl, virgin”), from Old English mǣġ (“kinswoman”), from Proto-West Germanic *māg, from Proto-Germanic *mēgaz (“kinsman”).
